::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## [P022] Wang et al. (2023) — Day-Ahead Optimal Bidding for a Retailer With Flexible Participation of Electric Vehicles

**Journal:** IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid, 14(2), 1482–1494, 2023  
**DOI:** 10.1109/TSG.2022.3208093  
**Main topics:** electric vehicles (EVs); distribution-level day-ahead energy market (DAEM); retailer bidding; incentive mechanism for charging (IMC); incentive mechanism for discharging (IMD); vehicle-to-grid (V2G); step bidding curves; conditional value at risk (CVaR); battery degradation; stochastic price scenarios

### Quick takeaway

This paper studies how a distribution-level electricity retailer should construct **day-ahead bidding curves** when a large population of electric vehicles can flexibly shift charging and, for some users, discharge energy back to the grid.

The central problem is:

**How can a retailer translate heterogeneous EV flexibility, user willingness, battery degradation, and uncertain day-ahead/real-time electricity prices into practical price-power bidding curves while controlling financial risk?**

The paper combines four main ideas:

- an **extended three-day investigating period** to capture EVs whose plug-in and plug-out times cross calendar-day boundaries;
- separate **incentive mechanisms for charging (IMC)** and **discharging (IMD)**;
- an explicit **step bidding-curve formulation** embedded in the retailer optimization problem;
- **CVaR-based risk aversion** under uncertain day-ahead and real-time prices.

The main message is that EV flexibility should not be treated simply as an aggregated fixed battery. Its market value depends on **when vehicles are connected, whether users are willing to participate, what compensation is required for battery degradation, and how the retailer bids into the market**.

---

### 1. Problem addressed

A retailer participates in a distribution-level day-ahead energy market by submitting a price-power bidding curve for each trading period of the next day.

The retailer serves two broad groups:

- **inflexible end users**, whose demand is assumed predictable;
- **flexible EV users**, whose charging and discharging behavior changes with prices and incentives.

The retailer therefore faces a more difficult problem than conventional demand forecasting:

**market prices affect EV behavior, and EV behavior affects the retailer's optimal market bid.**

This creates a feedback chain:

**market-price scenario → EV participation → charging/discharging schedule → retailer demand → bidding curve → market profit and imbalance risk**

---

### 2. Distribution-level day-ahead market framework

![Distribution-level DAEM framework in which retailers submit price-power bids to the independent system operator while serving inflexible and EV loads. Source: Fig. 1 of Wang et al. (2023).](papers/p022-wang2023-ev-day-ahead-bidding/figures/wang2023_ev_day_ahead_bidding/fig1_daem_framework.png){width=72%}

The retailer is modeled as a **price taker**.

Its trading volume is assumed too small to influence the market-clearing price.

Before the operation day, the retailer submits bidding curves to the day-ahead market. The independent system operator clears the market and determines:

- day-ahead purchase price;
- day-ahead traded power.

During real-time operation, deviations between actual load and day-ahead procurement are settled in the real-time market and may also incur imbalance penalties.

So the retailer earns money by selling electricity to end users, but pays for:

- day-ahead energy;
- real-time balancing energy;
- EV discharging compensation;
- imbalance penalties.

---

### 3. Why EVs complicate day-ahead bidding

EVs differ from conventional demand in several ways.

#### Temporal availability

An EV can only be controlled while plugged in.

#### Energy requirement

The vehicle must reach a required SOC before departure.

#### Bidirectional flexibility

If V2G is enabled and the user agrees, the EV can both charge and discharge.

#### User heterogeneity

Not every user is willing to delay charging or allow battery discharge.

#### Battery degradation

Discharging creates additional battery wear and therefore requires compensation.

#### Price responsiveness

The EV user's willingness to participate changes with potential savings or compensation.

The retailer therefore cannot assume that all connected EVs are fully controllable.

---

### 4. Three-stage uncertainty structure

![Three-stage scenario tree representing the bidding decision, day-ahead price realizations, and real-time price realizations. Source: Fig. 2 of Wang et al. (2023).](papers/p022-wang2023-ev-day-ahead-bidding/figures/wang2023_ev_day_ahead_bidding/fig2_three_stage_scenario_tree.png){width=67%}

The paper organizes uncertainty using a three-stage scenario tree.

#### Stage 1 — before day-ahead clearing

The retailer determines the **bidding curve**.

#### Stage 2 — day-ahead price realization

A day-ahead price scenario is realized.

This price affects:

- retail selling prices;
- EV charging participation;
- EV charging schedule;
- aggregated EV demand.

#### Stage 3 — real-time price realization

A real-time price scenario is realized.

The retailer settles deviations between actual demand and day-ahead purchased energy.

This allows the optimization to represent both:

**day-ahead bidding uncertainty + real-time imbalance uncertainty.**

---

### 5. A key modeling idea: the bidding horizon is not just one day

A major contribution is the treatment of EV temporal distribution.

For bidding on day \(n+1\), some EVs may already be connected on day \(n\), while others remain connected into day \(n+2\).

The paper therefore defines three EV types.

#### Type 1

Plug in on day \(n\), plug out on day \(n+1\).

#### Type 2

Plug in and plug out during day \(n+1\).

#### Type 3

Plug in on day \(n+1\), plug out on day \(n+2\).

![Three EV connection types and the resulting three-day investigating period for day-ahead bidding. Source: Fig. 3 of Wang et al. (2023).](papers/p022-wang2023-ev-day-ahead-bidding/figures/wang2023_ev_day_ahead_bidding/fig3_ev_temporal_distribution.png){width=70%}

Hence the optimization horizon spans:

**day \(n\) + day \(n+1\) + day \(n+2\)**

rather than treating each calendar day independently.

This is important because charging can be shifted across midnight.

---

### 6. Why the extended three-day period matters

Suppose an EV plugs in at 22:00 on day \(n\) and departs at 07:00 on day \(n+1\).

Its charging decision during the target day is already influenced by what happened before midnight.

Likewise, an EV plugging in at 20:00 on day \(n+1\) may postpone charging until early day \(n+2\).

A one-day model can therefore artificially truncate EV flexibility.

The paper avoids this boundary problem by explicitly extending the modeling horizon.

This is a useful general lesson for EV, thermal-load, storage, and other intertemporal flexibility models:

> **the optimization horizon should cover the physical flexibility window, not simply follow the market calendar.**

---

### 7. Incentive mechanism for charging (IMC)

The first flexibility mechanism concerns **charging-time shifting**.

After the day-ahead market is cleared, the retailer broadcasts time-varying selling prices.

The retail selling price is modeled as:

\[
\lambda^S_\omega(k)=\lambda^D_\omega(k)+\lambda^M_\omega(k)
\]

where:

- \(\lambda^D\): day-ahead electricity price;
- \(\lambda^M\): retailer's margin;
- \(\lambda^S\): selling price to EV users.

An EV user may enroll in the **Incentive Mechanism for Charging (IMC)**.

If enrolled:

> the retailer may shift charging within the available plug-in period to minimize the EV user's charging cost.

If not enrolled:

> the EV is charged immediately after plug-in until its required SOC is reached.

---

### 8. Charging participation is based on user willingness

The paper does not assume 100% participation.

The participation rate is represented as:

\[
\rho^{IMC}_\omega=f^{IMC}(\Delta\lambda^S_\omega)
\]

where \(\Delta\lambda^S\) is the peak-to-off-peak selling-price difference.

A larger price difference gives users more potential savings from delayed charging and therefore increases participation.

The relationship is obtained from **social-survey data**.

This is an important feature because the technically available flexibility of EVs is different from the **behaviorally available flexibility**.

---

### 9. Operation region of an individual EV

![Feasible SOC operation region of an EV considering charging, discharging, minimum/maximum SOC, and required departure SOC. Source: Fig. 4 of Wang et al. (2023).](papers/p022-wang2023-ev-day-ahead-bidding/figures/wang2023_ev_day_ahead_bidding/fig4_individual_ev_operation_area.png){width=58%}

The paper defines a feasible SOC region during each EV's connection period.

The upper boundary represents the fastest possible charging trajectory.

The lower boundary allows discharging down to the minimum SOC, followed by forced charging so that the EV still reaches the required departure SOC.

The actual EV trajectory must stay inside this feasible region.

This ensures that market participation never violates:

- battery SOC limits;
- charger power limits;
- required travel energy at departure.

---

### 10. Minimum required charging time

The minimum number of charging intervals is calculated from:

\[
k_i^{a0}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{Q_i(S_i^d-S_i^c)}{\eta_i^c P_i^{cr}\Delta k}
\right\rceil
\]

where:

- \(Q_i\): battery capacity;
- \(S_i^c\): initial SOC;
- \(S_i^d\): required departure SOC;
- \(P_i^{cr}\): rated charging power;
- \(\eta_i^c\): charging efficiency.

Without participation in the incentive mechanism, the EV is only considered controllable over this minimum charging period.

With participation, the available scheduling period can expand to the full connection period.

---

### 11. Incentive mechanism for discharging (IMD)

The second mechanism allows V2G discharging.

The paper recognizes that users are generally less willing to participate in discharging than in simple charging shifting because V2G introduces battery degradation.

The retailer therefore pays a compensation price:

\[
\lambda^C=\pi^0+\lambda^I
\]

where:

- \(\pi^0\): estimated unit battery degradation cost;
- \(\lambda^I\): additional incentive payment.

The total compensation must therefore cover battery wear plus an incentive that makes participation attractive.

---

### 12. Battery degradation is monetized

The paper estimates battery degradation from the relationship between:

- depth of discharge (DOD);
- battery cycle life.

For a given DOD, the lifetime processed energy is estimated.

An average lifetime throughput is then used to convert battery purchase cost into an approximate degradation cost per unit of discharged energy.

The result is a simplified linear unit cost:

\[
\pi_i^0 \propto
\frac{\text{battery purchase cost}}
{\text{lifetime processed energy}}
\]

This makes battery degradation directly usable in the market-bidding optimization.

---

### 13. IMC and IMD are behaviorally linked

The paper assumes that users who already join IMC are more motivated by economic benefits and are therefore more likely to join IMD.

The two participation mechanisms are consequently not treated as fully independent populations.

If the IMD participation rate is lower than the IMC participation rate:

> discharging participants are selected from IMC participants.

If IMD participation is higher:

> all IMC participants are assumed eligible, with additional participants included as needed.

This is a simple way to introduce correlation between users' willingness to shift charging and willingness to discharge.

---

### 14. EV users are guaranteed their minimum charging cost

A subtle but important idea is that flexible market scheduling should not make participating users worse off.

The paper first solves an **optimal charging model** to calculate the minimum charging cost that EV users could achieve under the incentive mechanism.

This minimum cost becomes the retailer's baseline selling income from EV users.

Then, in the retailer bidding model, EV charging/discharging may be further rearranged to improve market profit.

If this market-oriented rearrangement would increase the EV user's charging cost, the retailer is assumed to compensate for the difference.

So the retailer captures flexibility only while preserving the user's economic benefit.

---

### 15. Retailer's market-profit formulation

The retailer's profit contains the following major components:

**Revenue**

- energy-selling income from EVs;
- energy-selling income from inflexible users.

**Costs**

- day-ahead energy purchase;
- real-time balancing energy;
- EV discharging compensation;
- imbalance penalties.

The retailer therefore makes money by optimally coordinating:

**EV charging flexibility + V2G flexibility + DA procurement + RT correction.**

---

### 16. Step bidding curve is optimized directly

![Step price-power bidding curve used by the retailer in the day-ahead market. Source: Fig. 5 of Wang et al. (2023).](papers/p022-wang2023-ev-day-ahead-bidding/figures/wang2023_ev_day_ahead_bidding/fig5_step_bidding_curve.png){width=55%}

Rather than assuming a bidding curve externally, the paper embeds the curve itself in the optimization model.

The bidding curve consists of nodes:

\[
(P_1,\lambda_1),\ldots,(P_G,\lambda_G)
\]

with:

\[
P_1\ge P_2\ge\cdots\ge P_G
\]

and increasing price levels.

Thus:

- lower market prices correspond to larger desired purchase volumes;
- higher prices correspond to smaller desired purchase volumes.

This makes the optimization output directly usable as a practical market bid.

---

### 17. Why the bidding curve matters

A single optimal power value is not enough in a day-ahead market because the actual clearing price is not known when the bid is submitted.

The step bidding curve tells the market:

> **if the clearing price is low, I want this much energy; if the price is high, I want less.**

EV flexibility changes the shape of this demand-side bidding curve.

For example, if EV charging can be shifted away from expensive periods, the retailer can reduce its bid at high-price hours while increasing purchases during low-price hours.

---

### 18. Real-time imbalance and penalty cost

The actual EV demand may differ from the day-ahead purchase.

The retailer then uses the real-time market to balance the mismatch.

The model additionally applies penalties when imbalance exceeds specified thresholds.

This discourages a retailer from exploiting real-time balancing without adequately managing its day-ahead commitment.

Thus EV flexibility is valuable not only for energy arbitrage but also for:

**reducing day-ahead / real-time imbalance exposure.**

---

### 19. Why CVaR is introduced

Maximizing expected profit alone can produce aggressive bids that perform badly under unfavorable price scenarios.

The paper therefore uses **Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR)**.

At confidence level \(\alpha\), CVaR represents the expected profit in the worst \((1-\alpha)\times100\%\) scenarios.

The final objective combines:

\[
\text{Expected Profit}
+
\beta\times\text{CVaR}
\]

where \(\beta\) is the risk factor.

A larger \(\beta\) makes the retailer more risk averse.

---

### 20. Scenario construction in the case study

The paper uses historical NYISO data from June-August 2016-2020.

A total of 460 day-ahead and real-time price profiles are used.

The day-ahead profiles are reduced to:

**20 day-ahead price scenarios**

using k-means clustering.

For each day-ahead scenario, three real-time residual-price scenarios are generated.

Hence the final uncertainty set contains:

\[
20\times3=60
\]

price scenarios.

The test system contains **1,000 EVs** with heterogeneous connection times, SOCs, capacities, and charging parameters.

---

### 21. IMC changes the retailer's hourly bid

When only charging flexibility is enabled, the retailer shifts EV charging from expensive hours to cheaper hours.

For the reported example, relative to the reference case with no IMC participation, the retailer tends to:

- bid **more energy around hours 4-6**;
- bid **less energy from approximately hour 13 onward**.

This reflects the intended behavior:

**high-price charging → low-price charging.**

The value of EV flexibility is therefore visible directly in the day-ahead bidding curve.

---

### 22. Risk-aversion result

The paper varies the CVaR risk factor from 0 to 1.

Reported behavior:

- expected bidding profit decreases only slightly;
- bidding CVaR increases substantially.

Specifically, the paper reports that as the risk factor rises from 0 to 1:

- expected bidding profit decreases by about **$2.89**;
- bidding CVaR increases by about **$35.26**.

After the risk factor reaches roughly **0.4**, further changes in expected profit, CVaR, and the bidding curve become small.

This suggests that moderate risk aversion can substantially improve downside protection at relatively low expected-profit cost.

---

### 23. IMD has an economically optimal compensation range

Discharging compensation creates a non-monotonic trade-off.

If compensation is too low:

> users do not participate because battery degradation is not adequately covered.

If compensation is too high:

> V2G becomes too expensive for the retailer.

Therefore, there is an intermediate compensation range that maximizes retailer profit.

In the tested case, the highest reported profit occurs around a **$30/MWh compensation level** under the low battery-cost condition used in the simulation.

![Expected bidding profit under different compensation-price and battery-cost assumptions. Source: Fig. 10 of Wang et al. (2023).](papers/p022-wang2023-ev-day-ahead-bidding/figures/wang2023_ev_day_ahead_bidding/fig10_compensation_battery_profit.png){width=63%}

---

### 24. Better battery durability increases market value

As battery cycle life increases:

- unit degradation cost decreases;
- more users are willing to participate in IMD;
- V2G flexibility increases;
- retailer bidding profit increases.

The paper reports that profit grows strongly as cycle life increases from about **10,000 to 50,000 cycles**.

At very high cycle life, additional gains become small because participation becomes limited by other factors such as compensation willingness rather than battery degradation alone.

This shows that battery technology can directly change the economic value of EV participation in electricity markets.

---

### 25. More compensation does not necessarily mean more discharged energy

An interesting result appears in the compensation sensitivity analysis.

As compensation rises from low values:

- more users become willing to participate;
- retailer profit can initially increase.

But the retailer activates V2G only when the market-price spread is large enough to justify the compensation payment.

Therefore, with higher compensation:

> V2G may be economically attractive in fewer scenarios.

The paper reports that expected discharged energy decreases as the compensation price rises in the tested range, even while expected profit initially increases.

![Expected retailer profit and aggregate discharged energy under different compensation prices. Source: Fig. 12 of Wang et al. (2023).](papers/p022-wang2023-ev-day-ahead-bidding/figures/wang2023_ev_day_ahead_bidding/fig12_profit_discharge_compensation.png){width=63%}

---

### 26. What this paper teaches

#### Lesson 1 — EV flexibility is fundamentally intertemporal

The correct modeling horizon should cover full plug-in intervals, including those crossing midnight.

#### Lesson 2 — Technical flexibility and participating flexibility are different

An EV may physically be able to shift or discharge but the user may refuse.

Survey-based participation functions are therefore used to convert technical flexibility into behaviorally available flexibility.

#### Lesson 3 — Charging and discharging require different incentive designs

Simple charging delay primarily depends on electricity-price savings.

V2G additionally requires compensation for battery degradation and user inconvenience.

#### Lesson 4 — A practical market study should optimize the bidding curve itself

The paper does not stop at an optimal EV charging schedule.

It converts EV flexibility into an actual **day-ahead step bidding curve**.

#### Lesson 5 — Risk management changes the bidding curve

CVaR does not merely change a scalar profit metric.

It changes how much energy the retailer is willing to bid at different price levels.

#### Lesson 6 — Better batteries increase the market value of V2G

Longer cycle life lowers degradation cost and increases economically usable discharging flexibility.

---

### 27. Limitations

Important limitations include:

- the retailer is assumed to be a **price taker**;
- uncertainties in individual EV battery capacity, plug-in time, and charging rate are assumed predictable and their aggregate prediction error is neglected;
- user participation functions are derived from survey relationships and are not learned dynamically from actual repeated behavior;
- battery degradation is represented by a simplified unit-energy cost based mainly on DOD and cycle life;
- network constraints inside the distribution system are not the central focus of the retailer bidding model;
- EV user comfort, inconvenience, and mobility uncertainty are simplified into participation and SOC constraints;
- only day-ahead/real-time energy-market interactions are modeled rather than joint energy-reserve-ancillary-service participation;
- the study is scenario-based and depends on historical NYISO summer price data;
- the allocation of aggregate retailer profit back to individual EVs is not solved.

The authors explicitly identify **profit allocation among heterogeneous EVs according to contribution and uncertainty** as future work.

---

### 28. Critical reading notes

#### Battery-cost unit reporting should be checked carefully

The text discusses EV battery costs in the range of approximately **$200/kWh to $1260/kWh**, while parts of the simulation discussion/figures use a battery-cost axis or description in **$/MWh**.

Before reproducing the degradation-cost calculation, the unit convention should therefore be verified carefully from the equations, source data, and implementation.

#### Participation is exogenous to the optimization

The functions \(f^{IMC}(\cdot)\) and \(f^{IMD}(\cdot)\) are obtained from survey relationships.

This means the retailer optimizes *given* a behavioral participation model, rather than jointly learning behavior online.

#### Aggregation removes some individual uncertainty

The paper assumes that prediction errors in EV parameters can be ignored for a sufficiently large EV population.

This is convenient but may be optimistic in cases with correlated travel behavior, weather events, holidays, or concentrated charging demand.

---

### 29. Research idea triggers

Possible extensions include:

- online learning of IMC/IMD participation probabilities from actual customer responses;
- distributionally robust bidding under uncertain plug-in times, SOC, and participation;
- joint day-ahead energy + reserve + frequency-regulation bidding of EV aggregators;
- bi-level or game-theoretic bidding when the retailer is no longer a price taker;
- network-constrained bidding using DLMPs;
- fairness-aware allocation of V2G revenue among EV users;
- degradation-aware stochastic MPC for EV aggregation;
- personalized incentives rather than one common compensation price;
- dynamic contracts that distinguish high-flexibility and low-flexibility EV users;
- battery-health-aware participation using SOH estimation;
- learning-based bidding curves using historical market clearing data;
- coupling EV bidding with carbon prices or carbon-intensity signals;
- multi-retailer competition for EV flexibility;
- rolling day-ahead/intraday bidding instead of one-shot DA bidding.
